'''''Bidens frondosa''''' is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Asteraceae]]. It is an annual herb widespread across much of Canada and the United States.<ref name=grin>{{GRIN | accessdate = 4 January 2018 }}</ref><ref name="BF_FNA">{{EFloras|1|200023534|Bidens frondosa|first1=John L.|last1=Strother|first2=Ronald R.|last2=Weedon|volume=21|access-date=28 July 2025 }}</ref><ref>[http://bonap.net/MapGallery/State/Bidens%20frondosa.png Biota of North America Program 2014 state-level distribution map]</ref> It is known in many other parts of the world as an [[introduced species]], including Europe, Asia, Morocco, and New Zealand.<ref name=grin/><ref>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200023534 Flora of China, 大狼杷草 da lang pa cao, ''Bidens frondosa'' Linnaeus, Sp. Pl. 2: 832. 1753.]</ref><ref>[http://luirig.altervista.org/flora/taxa/index1.php?scientific-name=bidens+frondosa Altervista Flora Italiana, Forbicina fogliosa, schwarzfrüchtiger Zweizahn, ''Bidens frondosa'' L.]</ref> Its many common names include '''devil's beggarticks''', '''devil's-pitchfork''', '''devil's bootjack''', '''sticktights''', '''bur marigold''', '''pitchfork weed''', '''tickseed sunflower''',<ref name=itis>[https://www.itis.gov/servlet/SingleRpt/SingleRpt?search_topic=TSN&search_value=35707 ''Bidens frondosa''.] Integrated Taxonomic Information System (ITIS).</ref> '''leafy beggarticks''',<ref name=burke>[http://biology.burke.washington.edu/herbarium/imagecollection.php?Genus=Bidens&Species=frondosa ''Bidens frondosa''.] Burke Museum. University of Washington.</ref> and '''common beggar-ticks'''.<ref name=freck>[http://wisplants.uwsp.edu/scripts/detail.asp?SpCode=BIDFRO ''Bidens frondosa''.] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070702150725/http://wisplants.uwsp.edu/scripts/detail.asp?SpCode=BIDFRO |date=2 July 2007 }} Freckmann Herbarium. University of Wisconsin, Stevens Point.</ref>

== Description ==

''Bidens frondosa'' is an annual herb, usually growing to {{cvt|20-60|cm|in|0}} tall, but it may reach {{cvt|1.8|m|ft|0}}. The stems are square in cross-section and may branch near the top. The leaves are [[pinnate]], divided into a few toothed triangular or lance-shaped leaflets usually {{cvt|6-8|cm|in|frac=2}} long, exceptionally up to {{cvt|12|cm|in|frac=2}}. The [[inflorescence]] is often a solitary [[pseudanthium|flower head]], but there may be pairs or arrays of several heads. The head contains many orange [[disc floret]]s. Most flower heads lack [[ray florets]] but some may have a few small yellow rays. The fruit is a flat black or brown barbed [[Asteraceae#Fruits and seeds|cypsela]] up to a centimeter long which has two obvious hornlike [[pappus (flower structure)|pappi]] at one end.<ref name=BF_FNA/><ref name=burke/><ref name=vt>[http://www.ppws.vt.edu/scott/weed_id/bidfr.htm Devils Beggarticks or Stick-tights: ''Bidens frondosa''.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130624230508/http://www.ppws.vt.edu/scott/weed_id/bidfr.htm |date=24 June 2013 }} Virginia Tech Weed Identification Guide.</ref><ref>[http://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/cgi-bin/get_IJM.pl?tid=1702 ''Bidens frondosa''.] The Jepson eFlora 2013.</ref>

The barbed [[pappi]] on the fruit help it stick to animals, facilitating [[seed dispersal]].<ref name=vt/>

==Distribution and habitat==
''Bidens frondosa'' is [[Native species|native]] to northern North America. It is recorded as naturally occurring in the whole of the [[contiguous United States]] and Alaska, but not Montana, as well as all of Canada except for the three [[Northern Canada|Arctic territories]] and [[Labrador]].<ref name="POWO"/><ref name=BF_FNA/><ref name="vascan">{{cite journal |last1=Brouillet |first1=L |last2=Desmet |first2=P |last3=Coursol |first3=F |last4=Meades |first4=SJ |last5=Favreau |first5=M |last6=Anions |first6=M |last7=Bélisle |first7=P |last8=Gendreau |first8=C |last9=Shorthouse |first9=D |collaboration=VASCAN contributors |title=Bidens frondosa Linnaeus |url=https://data.canadensys.net/vascan/taxon/2934?lang=en |journal=PhytoKeys |date=2013 |issue=25 |pages=55–67 |publisher=Alliance de recherche numérique du Canada |access-date=28 July 2025 |doi=10.3897/phytokeys.25.3100 |pmid=24198712 |pmc=3819130 |doi-access=free }}</ref> It does not naturally occur south to Mexico,<ref name="POWO"/><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Villaseñor |first1=José Luis |title=Checklist of the native vascular plants of Mexico |journal=Revista mexicana de biodiversidad |date=September 2016 |volume=87 |issue=3 |pages=631–632 |doi=10.1016/j.rmb.2016.06.017 |doi-broken-date=29 July 2025 |url=https://www.scielo.org.mx/scielo.php?script=sci_arttext&pid=S1870-34532016000300559 |access-date=28 July 2025 |language=en |issn=1870-3453 |doi-access=free }}</ref> but it is recorded by [[CAB International|CABI]] as introduced there.<ref name="CABI">{{cite journal |last1=Popay |first1=I. |title=Bidens frondosa (beggarticks) |journal=CABI Compendium |date=3 April 2014 |volume=CABI Compendium |article-number=108916 |doi=10.1079/cabicompendium.108916 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

''Bidens frondosa'' has been widely [[Introduced species|introduced]] outside of North America, mostly in regions with [[temperate climate]]s. Most of these introductions have been intentional, because of the purported medicinal, herbal, and decorative properties of the species. In Italy, it was first introduced there in the 1700s as an ornamental plant, and was first reported as a [[Naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] weed in 1849.<ref name="Danuso">{{cite journal |last1=Danuso |first1=Francesco |last2=Zanin |first2=Giuseppe |last3=Sartorato |first3=Ivan |title=A modelling approach for evaluating phenology and adaptation of two congeneric weeds (Bidens frondosa and Bidens tripartita) |journal=Ecological Modelling |date=24 September 2012 |volume=243 |pages=33–41 |doi=10.1016/j.ecolmodel.2012.06.009 |bibcode=2012EcMod.243...33D |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0304380012002815 |access-date=28 July 2025 |issn=0304-3800 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> It is widespread across Europe, where it has been reported from almost every country except for Finland, Sweden, and Greece. In Asia, it has been reported from the Middle East (Iran, Lebanon, Syria, Turkey), the [[Caucasus]], Central Asia and [[Western Siberia]], China, Korea, Japan, and the [[Russian Far East]]. It has also been introduced to New Zealand and Morocco.<ref name="POWO"/><ref name="CABI"/>

''Bidens frondosa'' grows best where there is ample soil moisture and sun, especially in areas where something has disrupted the existing plant community leaving bare ground. It can survive in water saturated soils, frequently found growing at the water's edge, in drainage ditches or on flood plains.<ref name="Hilty">{{cite web |last1=Hilty |first1=John |title=Common Beggar-Ticks (Bidens frondosa) |url=http://www.illinoiswildflowers.info/wetland/plants/cm_beggarticks.htm |access-date=11 October 2018 |website=www.illinoiswildflowers.info }}</ref><ref name="CABI"/>

==Ecology==
The defoliating [[caterpillar]] of ''[[Hadjina chinensis]]'', which is limited to ''Bidens'' species, has been observed on this plant.<ref>Han, Y. G., et al. (2009). [http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1748-5967.2009.00253.x/abstract?deniedAccessCustomisedMessage=&userIsAuthenticated=false Insect herbivores associated with the introduced weed ''Bidens frondosa'' L.(Asteraceae) in Korea, and their potential role as augmentative biological control agents.] ''Entomological Research'' 39(6), 394-400.</ref>

===Invasiveness===
This plant is [[invasive species|invasive]] in some parts of the world. It is also weedy in its native range, occurring in pastures and fields and along roadsides.<ref name=vt/> 
In New Zealand it is classed as an environmental weed by the [[Department of Conservation (New Zealand)|Department of Conservation]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Howell |first=C. |title=Consolidated List of Environmental Weeds in New Zealand |publisher=Department of Conservation |location=Wellington, New Zealand |date=May 2008 |series=292 |isbn=978-0-478-14413-0 }}</ref>

Across [[Eurasia]], this species is a problematic environmental and agricultural weed that threatens native species of ''Bidens'' through [[Competition (biology)|competition]] and [[genetic pollution]].<ref name="CABI"/> Populations of the native ''[[Bidens tripartita]]'' and ''[[Bidens radiata]]'' have been recorded as declining and disappearing in the presence of the alien ''B. frondosa'', which can also interbreed with these species, replacing them with hybrids.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Vasilyeva |first1=N. V. |last2=Papchenkov |first2=V. G. |title=Mechanisms of influence of invasive Bidens frondosa L. on indigenous Bidens species |journal=Russian Journal of Biological Invasions |date=1 October 2011 |volume=2 |issue=2–3 |page=81 |doi=10.1134/S2075111711020123 |bibcode=2011RuJBI...2...81V |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1134/S2075111711020123 |access-date=28 July 2025 |language=en |issn=2075-1125 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> Studies comparing ''B. frondosa'' with ''B. tripartita'' and ''B. radiata'' in the [[Ural Mountains|Middle Urals]] show that ''B. frondosa'' plants have larger sizes, higher seed production, and greater biomass, indicating their high competitive ability.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ronzhina |first1=D. A. |title=Distribution, competitive ability, and seed production of Bidens frondosa L. in the Middle Urals |journal=Russian Journal of Biological Invasions |date=1 October 2017 |volume=8 |issue=4 |pages=351–359 |doi=10.1134/S2075111717040099 |bibcode=2017RuJBI...8..351R |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1134/S2075111717040099 |access-date=28 July 2025 |language=en |issn=2075-1125 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> In Italy, where it is a rapidly spreading agricultural weed in the [[Po Valley]], studies of the [[phenology]] of ''B. frondosa'' with ''B. tripartita'' suggest that its invasive capacity could be related to the length of its vegetative phase, allowing it to be more adaptable and permitting greater growth by delaying reproductive development.<ref name="Danuso"/> A comparison of the two species in China also suggests that ''B. frondosa'' has a higher phenotypic plasticity in response to water and nitrogen addition relative to ''B. tripartita'', and that future increases in precipitation in China and atmospheric nitrogen deposition will increase its invasiveness.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wei |first1=Chunqiang |last2=Tang |first2=Saichun |last3=Pan |first3=Yumei |last4=Li |first4=Xiangqin |title=Plastic responses of invasive Bidens frondosa to water and nitrogen addition |journal=Nordic Journal of Botany |date=2017 |volume=35 |issue=2 |pages=232–239 |doi=10.1111/njb.01331 |bibcode=2017NorJB..35..232W |url=https://nsojournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1111/njb.01331 |access-date=28 July 2025 |language=en |issn=1756-1051 |url-access=subscription }}</ref>
